title: Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 1)
hookLine: a woman prays so hard the priest thinks she's drunk

lines: HOW LONG WILT THOU BE DRUNKEN?
ELI, BY A POST AT SHILOH.
cards: "How long wilt thou be drunken? put away thy wine from thee." That's a priest, speaking to a woman at prayer. His name is Eli, and he's sitting by a post of the temple of the LORD at Shiloh, watching her.
Her lips are moving. No sound comes out. So he decides she's had too much at the family's meal.

He couldn't be more wrong. The first book of Samuel doesn't open with a king or a battle. It opens with a woman who can't have children, a family trip to worship, and a prayer so deep it looks like a scandal.

teach.h: AM NOT I BETTER TO THEE THAN TEN SONS?
teach.b: Back up. Hannah's husband, Elkanah, has two wives. "Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children."
Every year at Shiloh, the text says, her rival provoked her sore, until Hannah wept and couldn't eat.

Elkanah loves her, and tries: "Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?" Yesterday the women told Naomi that Ruth was better than seven sons.
Here a husband asks if he's better than ten, and the text gives no answer from her. Hannah gets up and goes to pray. "She was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore."
She vows: if God will remember her and give her a son, she'll give him back to the LORD all his life.
Then: "Hannah, she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard: therefore Eli thought she had been drunken." When he scolds her, she doesn't flinch.

teach.h: I HAVE POURED OUT MY SOUL.
teach.b: "No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD." Poured out, like water from a jar, nothing kept back.
Eli changes his mind at once: "Go in peace," and may God grant your petition.

teach.h: NO MORE SAD, BEFORE ANYTHING CHANGED.
teach.b: And here's the detail to carry: Hannah goes and eats, and "her countenance was no more sad." She isn't pregnant yet. Nothing has changed.
Only the jar is empty. Later she has a son and names him Samuel, "Because I have asked him of the LORD." And she keeps her vow.

how: Some Christians turn to Hannah's story when they pray about longing, infertility or grief, and read her silent prayer in 1 Samuel 1 alongside her song of thanks in 1 Samuel 2.

o: a silent prayer that poured out her whole soul
a written vow left at the temple door
a loud public prayer that the priest led

games.q: Hannah at Shiloh — tap the pairs.
p: provoked her sore, to make her fret
better to thee than ten sons?

s: Hannah prayed aloud, weeping, so Eli heard every word
she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard (1 Samuel 1:13).
Eli changed his mind once Hannah explained herself
he said, go in peace, and may God grant your petition (1:17).
Hannah's sadness lifted only after her son was born
her countenance was no more sad right after she prayed, before anything changed (1:18).

games.q: you're Hannah, praying silently at Shiloh. the priest accuses you of being drunk. what do you say?
o: no, my lord. I have poured out my soul before the LORD.
tell him off for judging a stranger.
games.why: she answers him plainly: a woman of a sorrowful spirit, not drunk, pouring out her soul. and Eli blesses her.

practice: Let whatever's heaviest come up, the thing you want and don't have, the thing that keeps hurting, without shaping it into sentences; Hannah's voice wasn't heard.
Let your breath carry it out slowly, like tipping a jar until it's empty, and notice what's left. If you pray, do this before God.

wordCard.voice: Hannah's prayer. A silent prayer at Shiloh, so deep the priest thought she was drunk. She poured out her soul before the LORD, and went home no more sad.

carryVoice: Your line: poured out before the lord. Her face changed before anything else did. See you tomorrow.
